notes:
Here are my verse-by-verse notes on Mark 9:26–50, drawn from the sources I was able to reach. Where I could not find material from particular traditions, I note that at the end.

---

## Mark 9:26–29 — The Demon Cast Out and the Disciples' Question

**v. 26:** After shrieking and convulsing him violently, the spirit came out. The boy became like a corpse, so that many said, “He is dead.”

Ellicott notes that the verb translated “rent him sore” (KJV) is the same as the “tare him” of Mark 9:20 and implies a spasm of horror convulsing the whole frame. The corpse-like falling, the cry of “the many” (i.e., most of them) that he was dead, and Jesus taking the boy by the hand are details peculiar to Mark’s Gospel. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/mark-9.html)

David Guzik (Enduring Word) comments that the demon, knowing it must leave, did the most damage it could before departing—but it was not lasting damage. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-9/)

**v. 27:** But Jesus took him by the hand and helped him to his feet, and he stood up.

Ellicott notes that Jesus’ taking the boy by the hand is a detail reported only by Mark. It demonstrates Jesus’ compassionate, personal touch following the violent exorcism. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/mark-9.html)

**v. 28:** After Jesus had gone into the house, His disciples asked Him privately, “Why couldn’t we drive it out?”

The StudyLight verse-by-verse commentary observes that it was well for the apostles’ reputation that they sought a private answer, for they were grievously at fault. Matthew quoted Jesus as saying their failure was due to “little faith” (Matthew 17:20), and Mark indicates either a failure to pray at all or a serious lack in their prayers. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/mark/9-29.html)

Dr. Constable’s Expository Notes (StudyLight) suggest the nine disciples believed the power Jesus had given them was now inherent in themselves. It was not; it was still God’s power coming directly from Him. They needed to acknowledge their dependence on God. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/mark-9.html)

**v. 29:** Jesus answered, “This kind cannot come out, except by prayer.”

*Note: Some manuscripts add “and fasting” (reflected in the KJV); the earliest and best manuscripts omit those words, as Ellicott notes.* (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/mark-9.html)

Ellicott observes that “and fasting” is missing from the better MSS, and may have been added later (like “with tears” in v.24) from an ascetic tendency in the early church. However, he also notes that in Matthew both words appear and that what they teach is in harmony with other portions of the teaching of Christ and His Apostles. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/mark-9.html)

David Guzik: “It isn’t that prayer and fasting make us more worthy to cast out demons. It is that prayer and fasting draw us closer to the heart of God, and they put us more in line with His power. They are an expression of our total dependence on Him.” He quotes Wiersbe: “The authority that Jesus had given them was effective only if exercised by faith, but faith must be cultivated through spiritual discipline and devotion.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-9/)

GotQuestions.org explains that the core issue is a heart humbly seeking God. Some manuscripts include “and fasting,” and many believers have found fasting deepens focus on God, yet the core issue remains humble dependence. (https://www.gotquestions.org/only-come-out-by-prayer-and-fasting.html)

JFB (Jamieson-Fausset-Brown) notes that Jesus’ answer in Matthew 17:20-21 is fuller: “Because of your unbelief … Howbeit this kind goeth not out but by prayer and fasting”—meaning that though nothing is impossible to faith, such a height of faith is not reached either in a moment or without effort—either with God in prayer or with ourselves in self-denying exercises. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/mark/9.htm)

---

## Mark 9:30–32 — Second Prediction of the Passion

**v. 30:** Going on from there, they passed through Galilee. But Jesus did not want anyone to know…

Guzik: This was probably because Jesus did not want the Galilean multitude to cling to Him and hinder this important trip to Jerusalem. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-9/)

The Pulpit Commentary (on biblehub) notes that they passed through Galilee “not through the cities, but by them, in the most private ways”—Jesus sought seclusion to instruct His disciples without interruption. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mark/9-30.htm)

**v. 31:** …He was teaching His disciples. He told them, “The Son of Man will be delivered into the hands of men. They will kill Him, and after three days He will rise.”

JFB notes the use of the present tense “is delivered”—as Bengel says, steps were already in course of being taken to bring it about. The antithesis “the Son of man shall be delivered into the hands of men” is worthy of notice and appears in all three Synoptic Gospels. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/mark/9.htm)

The Pulpit Commentary: “The whole is present to his mind, as though it were now taking place.” Our Lord repeats this prediction so that when these events took place, the disciples might not abandon their faith as though He could not be the Messiah because He underwent so terrible a death. (https://biblehub.com/mark/9-31.htm)

Guzik: Jesus clearly told His disciples of this destiny back in Mark 8:31. Now, as they departed from Galilee towards Jerusalem, they headed towards the destiny Jesus spoke of. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-9/)

**v. 32:** But they did not understand this statement, and they were afraid to ask Him about it.

JFB: “Their most cherished ideas were so completely dashed by such announcements, that they were afraid of laying themselves open to rebuke by asking Him any questions. But ‘they were exceeding sorry’ (Mt 17:23).” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/mark/9.htm)

Gill: They could not understand how it could be—how so holy and innocent a man could be put to death, or how this could consist with His character as Son of God and Messiah, given their notions of the Messiah’s abiding forever and setting up a temporal kingdom. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mark/9-32.htm)

The Expositor’s Greek Testament (on biblehub) notes: “What they were ignorant of was the why, the δεῖ. With all He had said, Jesus had not yet been able to make that plain. They will never know till the Passion has become a fact accomplished.” It adds poignantly: “ἐφοβοῦντο, they feared to ask, they did not wish to understand, they would live on in hope.” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mark/9-32.htm)

---

## Mark 9:33–37 — Who Is the Greatest?

**v. 33:** Then they came to Capernaum. While Jesus was in the house, He asked them, “What were you discussing on the way?”

The Pulpit Commentary: Jesus overheard the debate on the road but waited until they were alone in the house to inquire, so He could address all twelve. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mark/9-33.htm)

**v. 34:** But they were silent, for on the way they had been arguing about which of them was the greatest.

Guzik: “This was an embarrassed silence. It showed that they were ashamed of their obsession with greatness. It was a healthy sense of shame and proved that some of the message of Jesus was sinking into their hearts.” He adds: “It seems that this was the favorite debating topic among the disciples.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-9/)

Ellicott: “Better, more simply, who was the greatest.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/mark-9.html)

**v. 35:** Sitting down, Jesus called the Twelve and said, “If anyone wants to be first, he must be the last of all and the servant of all.”

Guzik notes that sitting down was the posture of a Rabbi formally teaching. He observes: “For an example of greatness, Jesus put forth the last and the servant … He was truly first yet made Himself last of all and servant of all for our sake.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-9/)

Precept Austin, on the parallel in Matthew 18, explains that Jesus’ teaching overturns worldly ambition: “True greatness in God’s kingdom is found not in self-exaltation but in self-lowering, serving others, and fully relying on God’s grace.” (https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-18-commentary)

**v. 36:** Then He had a little child stand among them. Taking the child in His arms, He said to them…

Ellicott notes that the Greek participle for “taking him in his arms” occurs only here and in Mark 10:16. It may mean the child was taken up in our Lord’s arms, or that the arms were folded around him—the latter is somewhat more probable. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/mark-9.html)

**v. 37:** “Whoever welcomes one of these little children in My name welcomes Me, and whoever welcomes Me welcomes not only Me, but the One who sent Me.”

Ellicott: “The climax carries the truth to its completion. When we love a little child in the name of Christ, i.e., for His sake, and after His manner, we are sharers in His spirit, and when we love or receive Him who was one with the Father, we enter into fellowship with Him who is the Supreme and Eternal Love.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/mark-9.html)

Guzik: “True greatness isn’t cliquish; it has an inclusive instinct.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-9/)

---

## Mark 9:38–41 — The Unknown Exorcist

**v. 38:** John said to Him, “Teacher, we saw someone else driving out demons in Your name, and we tried to stop him, because he does not accompany us.”

Ligonier (Reformed): “John’s protest showed that something was wrong with his understanding. The complaint was that the man ‘was not following us,’ not that he ‘was not following You, Jesus.’ John had a misplaced sense of priorities.” The disciples were focused on exclusivity in an unhealthy way—each wanted to be the “greatest,” and this exclusionary attitude operated on a group level too. (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/side-jesus)

Calvin (on ccel.org): “There is reason to suspect the disciples of Christ of ambition, because they are anxious to maintain their privilege and honor. For how comes it that they all at once forbid a man who is unknown to them to work miracles, but because they wish to be the sole possessors of this right?” (https://ccel.org/study/Mark_9:38-41)

Ellicott: The incident is historically significant—it shows that Jesus’ work had stirred up spiritual powers in men outside the circle of disciples. “They believed in Him, or they would not have used His Name. They were fellow-workers with Him.” The case stands on an entirely different footing from the sons of Sceva in Acts 19:13-14. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/mark-9.html)

**v. 39:** “Do not stop him,” Jesus replied. “For no one who performs a miracle in My name can turn around and speak evil of Me.”

Ligonier/Sproul: Jesus called John to evaluate the man’s relationship to Christ not on the basis of the group to which he belonged but on the basis of the fruit of his ministry. The man was bearing good fruit, so he should not have been treated as outside the kingdom. (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/side-jesus)

Barnes’ Notes: “He to whom God gave the power of working a miracle, by that gave evidence that he could not be found among the enemies of Jesus.” The word rendered “lightly” (KJV) means quickly or immediately. He would not soon afterward speak evil of Christ. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mark/9-40.htm)

**v. 40:** “For whoever is not against us is for us.”

JFB: “Two principles of immense importance are here laid down: ‘First, No one will readily speak evil of Me who has the faith to do a miracle in My name; and second, If such a person cannot be supposed to be against us, ye are to consider him for us.’” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mark/9-40.htm)

The Pulpit Commentary (biblehub) notes the apparent tension with Matthew 12:30 (“He that is not with me is against me”). Dr. Morison explains: “When in applied morals we sit in judgment on ourselves, we should in ordinary circumstances apply the law obversely and stringently, ‘he who is not with Christ is against him.’ But when we are sitting in judgment on others, into whose hearts we cannot look directly, we should in ordinary circumstances apply the law reversely and leniently, ‘he who is not against Christ is for him.’” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mark/9-40.htm)

Calvin: “He only affirms that they act improperly, who unseasonably prevent the kingdom of God from being advanced by any means whatever. And yet he does not acknowledge as his disciples, or reckon as belonging to his flock, those who hold an intermediate place between enemies and friends, but means that, so far as they do no harm, they are useful and profitable.” (https://ccel.org/study/Mark_9:38-41)

Ligonier/Sproul cautions: “We must be careful to draw boundaries only on essential matters and be willing to work with those who truly belong to Christ even if they are not part of our particular group or congregation.” At the same time, we must avoid the error of thinking no division is important—denying the deity of Christ, adding works to justification, or advocating lawless living does mark someone as outside genuine faith. (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/side-jesus)

**v. 41:** “Indeed, if anyone gives you even a cup of water because you bear the name of Christ, truly I tell you, he will never lose his reward.”

Ellicott notes this is a reproduction of a promise from Matthew 10:42 in a different context, significant as an instance of our Lord’s method of teaching—reiterating words of blessing until they were engraved on the disciples’ minds. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/mark-9.html)

Guzik: “A small cup of water given in Jesus’ name is eternally remembered by God.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-9/)

---

## Mark 9:42 — The Millstone Warning

**v. 42:** “But if anyone causes one of these little ones who believe in Me to stumble, it would be better for him to have a large millstone hung around his neck and to be thrown into the sea.”

Gill: “Christ is not speaking of little children in age, who are neither capable of believing in Christ, nor are they ready to take offence; but of such as belong to him; his disciples and followers.” The “little ones” are believers who are humble and lowly. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mark/9-42.htm)

JFB: The “offence” (causing to stumble) refers probably to the effect which such unsavory disputes as the disciples had held would have upon the inquiring and hopeful who came in contact with them, leading them to believe that after all, Jesus’ followers were no better than others. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mark/9-42.htm)

The Cambridge Bible notes: the millstone (μύλος ὀνικός) is literally an “ass-mill-stone”—a millstone so large as to require turning by an ass, far heavier than a hand-mill. This was not a Jewish punishment but was in use among the Greeks, Romans, Syrians, and Phoenicians. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mark/9-42.htm)

Matthew Henry: “Whosoever shall grieve any true Christians, though they be of the weakest, shall oppose their entrance into the ways of God, or discourage and obstruct their progress … his punishment will be very great, and the death and ruin of his soul more terrible than such a death and ruin of his body would be.” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/mark/9.htm)

The Pulpit Commentary: “This verse stands out as the severe antithesis to what has gone before. As he who receives and encourages Christ’s little ones … receives him, and so shall receive from him the glorious rewards of Heaven; so, on the contrary, whosoever shall offend one of these little ones that believe in Christ is guilty of deadly sin.” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mark/9-42.htm)

---

## Mark 9:43–48 — Radical Self-Denial and Gehenna

*Note: vv. 44 and 46 (“where their worm dieth not, and the fire is not quenched”) are not found in the oldest and best manuscripts and are omitted from the BSB and most modern translations except the KJV/NKJV. As Ellicott notes, the best MSS omit both vv.44 and 46, leaving v.48 as the only description of Gehenna in this passage.* (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/mark-9.html)

**v. 43:** “If your hand causes you to sin, cut it off. It is better for you to enter life crippled than to have two hands and go into hell, into the unquenchable fire.”

Ellicott: “Into hell—Better, Gehenna, to distinguish it from the other word ‘Hades,’ also translated ‘Hell.’” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/mark-9.html)

Matthew Henry: “This charity must begin at home; if we must take heed of doing any thing to hinder others from good, and to occasion their sin, much more careful must we be to avoid every thing that will take us off from our duty, or lead us to sin; and that which doth so we must part with, though it be ever so dear to us.” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/mark/9.htm)

**v. 47:** “And if your eye causes you to sin, pluck it out. It is better for you to enter the kingdom of God with one eye than to have two eyes and be thrown into hell…”

Meyer’s Commentary (on biblehub) notes the literary structure: in the three references to everlasting torment, it is only at the end, in the case of the third (the eye, v.47), that the awful “where their worm does not die and the fire is not quenched” (v.48) comes in and “affectingly winds up the representation.” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mark/9-42.htm)

**v. 48:** “where ‘their worm never dies, and the fire is never quenched.’”

Ellicott: The words are taken almost literally from the closing verse of Isaiah (66:24). The imagery of putrid carcasses and blazing fires was already familiar. He explains: “Well-nigh all Christian thinkers have seen in the gnawing worm, the anguish of an endless remorse, the memory of past sins. Fire retains its wonted force as the expression of the righteousness of God manifesting itself to the consciousness of the sinner in all its awfulness, purifying where there is any desire, and therefore capacity, for purification, but never altering its essential character.” He adds: “So much the words declare distinctly, as the law of righteous retribution. They do not absolutely exclude the thought that the fire may consume or destroy that which it cannot purify; still less do they affirm that it will.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/mark-9.html)

Matthew Henry (Concise): “Doubtless, remorse of conscience and keen self-reflection are this never-dying worm.” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mark/9-49.htm)

Meyer notes that against a literal understanding of the worm and fire, it may be urged that the two together are incompatible (in reality, worms and fire cannot coexist), and that “salt” in v.49—the counterpart of “fire”—is clearly figurative. The whole is a figurative designation of the painful and endless punishments of hell. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mark/9-42.htm)

---

## Mark 9:49 — Salted with Fire

**v. 49:** “For everyone will be salted with fire.”

Ellicott outlines two main interpretations:

(1) **The traditional “preservation in judgment” view:** Salt symbolises perpetuation. The words become an emphatic assertion of the endlessness of future punishment—the lost are “salted with fire” so that they endure forever in torment. Against this, Ellicott objects that (a) it arbitrarily limits “every one” only to the condemned; (b) it is scarcely conceivable that “salted” would be used in such contrasted senses in the same verse; and (c) the uniform biblical symbolism of salt as purifying and preserving from corruption (Matthew 5:13; Leviticus 2:13) argues against this application.

(2) **The purifying/discipline view:** Fire represents the righteousness of God manifested as punishing and chastising—the discipline of suffering (as in Matthew 3:11, “baptism with the Holy Ghost and with fire”; 1 Corinthians 3:13; 1 Peter 1:7). “Of that discipline, our Lord says ‘every one’ shall be a partaker. He shall thus be ‘salted with fire,’ for the tendency of that fire, the aim of the sufferings which it represents, is to purify and cleanse.”

Ellicott concludes that the second clause (“and every sacrifice shall be salted with salt,” found in some MSS) refers back to Leviticus 2:13, where salt was added to every sacrifice as a symbol of incorruption. The spiritual sacrifice each believer offers needs both the fire of discipline and the salt of the Holy Spirit’s purifying grace. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/mark-9.html)

Barnes’ Notes: “Perhaps no passage in the New Testament has given more perplexity to commentators than this, and it may be impossible now to fix its precise meaning.” He records two common views: (a) salt preserves, so fire will preserve the wicked in existence for continual suffering; (b) as salt was sprinkled on the victim preparatory to sacrifice (Leviticus 2:13), so the apostles, by fiery trials, would be prepared as a sacrifice to God. Barnes leans toward the latter, suggesting the passage may have no reference to future punishment at all. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mark/9-49.htm)

MacLaren’s Expositions (biblehub): “There is a fire that destroys, and there is a fire that preserves; and the alternative for every man is to choose between the destructive and the conserving influences. Christian disciples have to submit to be ‘salted with fire,’ lest a worse thing befall them.” MacLaren identifies the “salting fire” primarily as the fire of the Divine Spirit—the Holy Spirit who cleanses and preserves by burning away sin. He also includes the fiery trials and outward disciplines of life as part of this salting process. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mark/9-49.htm)

Benson Commentary: Takes “every one” to refer specifically to those who will not cut off offending members and are consequently cast into hell—they are “salted with fire” meaning preserved, not consumed, thereby enduring forever. The second half (“every sacrifice shall be salted with salt”) refers to believers who offer themselves as living sacrifices, seasoned with divine grace. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mark/9-49.htm)

---

## Mark 9:50 — Salt and Peace

**v. 50:** “Salt is good, but if the salt loses its saltiness, with what will you season it? Have salt among yourselves, and be at peace with one another.”

Ellicott: The primary reference here is to the inward grace of which salt is the symbol, and which alone makes the Church what it ought to be as “the salt of the earth.” The command “have peace in yourselves” (or “among yourselves”) seems to refer back to the contention in vv.33-34 with which this whole portion of teaching began: “The purity from selfish aims, which was symbolised by the ‘salt,’ was the chief or only preservative of peace.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/mark-9.html)

Matthew Henry (Concise): “Like the sacrifices, we must be salted with salt; our corrupt affections must be subdued and mortified by the Holy Spirit. Those that have the salt of grace, must show they have a living principle of grace in their hearts, which works out corrupt dispositions in the soul that would offend God, or our own consciences.” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mark/9-49.htm)

Benson: The closing exhortation “have peace one with another” is a direct rebuke to the disciples’ dispute about who was the greatest—the salt of grace should produce peace, not rivalry. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mark/9-49.htm)

---

## Where Protestant Traditions Differ

Due to search and fetch limits, I could not retrieve tradition-specific material for most verses. I draw attention to some discernible differences from what was found:

- **v.29 “prayer and fasting”:** Pentecostal and charismatic traditions (e.g., Enduring Word, which draws broadly from evangelical and charismatic sources) tend to emphasise the practical power of combined prayer and fasting for spiritual warfare. Reformed commentators (e.g., Constable, Ellicott) tend to note the textual question and focus on dependence on God rather than ascetical practice. I did not find specific Methodist/Wesleyan or Lutheran pages on this verse.

- **vv.43–48 (radical amputation language):** Conservative evangelical teachers (Gill, Henry, JFB) treat these as hyperbolic expressions calling for decisive renunciation of sin, while affirming the reality of hell. The question of whether the language is literal or figurative is universally answered as figurative (no mainstream tradition teaches literal self-mutilation). I could not reach tradition-specific pages from Baptist (Desiring God, GTY), Methodist (Seedbed), Lutheran (LCMS, 1517), or Pentecostal sources.

- **v.49 “salted with fire”:** This verse is a known point of divergence. The “preservation for eternal torment” interpretation (Benson, some traditional readings) contrasts with the “purifying discipline” interpretation (Ellicott, MacLaren). Catholic and Orthodox readings (see below) sometimes connect this to purgatorial fire. I could not retrieve dedicated Baptist, Reformed, or Pentecostal statements.

- **v.40 “whoever is not against us is for us”:** Ligonier (Reformed/Sproul) emphasises boundary-drawing with wisdom—neither overly inclusive nor exclusively narrow. Calvin’s commentary (ccel.org) emphasises that Christ does not acknowledge these independent exorcists as disciples but says they are useful insofar as they do no harm. I could not retrieve Baptist, Methodist, or Pentecostal takes.

---

## Other Views

**Catholic and Orthodox readings:** I was unable to reach newadvent.org, catholic.com, or oca.org due to search/fetch limits. However, Ellicott’s discussion of v.49 notes that the “purifying fire” interpretation—fire as cleansing discipline—has affinities with the Catholic doctrine of purgatory, though Ellicott himself does not make that connection. Orthodox commentators sometimes read “salted with fire” in connection with theosis (purification by divine fire).

**Modern scholarship:** I could not reach bibleodyssey.org or netbible.org due to limits. The NET Bible notes (netbible.org) would typically address the textual issues in vv.29, 44, 46, and 49. From the older critical scholarship reported in Meyer’s and Ellicott, the main issues are: (a) “and fasting” in v.29 is a later scribal addition; (b) vv.44 and 46 are not original to Mark; (c) the second clause of v.49 is also textually disputed.
